dct_description_sm: Following calving, dairy cows are exposed to multiple stressors, including pain, unstable social groups and separation from their calf. How these stressors affect mood states and how such effects evolve over time remain poorly understood. We investigated the effects of cow-calf contact duration before separation and time post-calving on dairy cows’ mood states, assessed through reward sensitivity and responses to reward loss. Holstein cows (n = 18; 2.9 ± 1.09 years old) were randomly allocated to either 1) cow-calf contact for 3 d before separation or 2) a control treatment, in which cows were separated from their calf within 5 h of birth. At approximately 4 d and 30 d post-calving, cows were subjected to Successive Negative Contrast (SNC) tests. Cows were first trained to approach a 0.5 kg grain reward over 3 trials per session until they reach a learning criterion, or completed a maximum of 7 sessions. The grain reward was then reduced to 0.1 kg/trial for 5 sessions. During the first SNC test, cows kept with their calf for 3 days were slower to reach the initial reward after separation than control cows. Following the reward reduction, approach latencies increased for both treatments, but cow-calf contact cows were more likely to exhibit slow approaches, indicating stronger response to the loss of reward. At one month post-calving, cow-calf contact cows remained more likely to show slow approaches to the reduced reward than control cows. Individual responses to reward loss were positively correlated across tests, suggesting individual consistency in responses to reward loss over time. Overall, cows that remained with their calf for 3 d showed lower reward sensitivity and stronger responses to reward loss than control cows, consistent with anhedonia-like responses and more negative mood states. These effects persisted for up to one month post-calving, and, together with the observed individual consistency over time, suggest that early post-partum stressors may have lasting effects on dairy cows’ mood states.
